Customer briefings (00-brief.md)

Brief

Verbatim (user, 2026-10-13)

For later: When you are done we want a browser clone of diablo the famous hack and slay as a tribute but in an office environment. For building it stay close to the original and as input use an agent to play my role while i am not here - put it into a separate folder and use it to test and improve the coding harness we are building

(Typos corrected only where the meaning was unambiguous: "Dor builind" → "For building", "inti a seperate filder" → "into a separate folder", "harbess we arw buildf" → "harness we are building".)

Restatement

Build a playable browser game that pays tribute to the original isometric action-RPG classic: real-time click-to-move combat, a safe town hub, randomly generated dungeon levels going deeper, monsters, loot with randomised properties, character stats and skills, health/mana potions, an inventory. The setting is an office. Stay close to the original's mechanics and feel. Use original names, art, text and story (see claims). The project lives in its own folder and is built through the harness, with an agent playing the user's role, so the harness gets tested and improved on a real project.

Claims

#ClaimStatusNote
G1A browser clone of the original, as a tributesupported as a genre tributeMechanics, structure and feel can be reproduced. Calling it a clone of the named game, or using its name, would not be
G2Stay close to the originalpartly contradictedClose in mechanics: yes. The original's names, characters, artwork, music, text, logo and trade dress belong to their owner. Harness rule 06 forbids copying them. All of these are original here
G3An agent plays the user's role while they are awaysupportedcustomer-proxy agent; every answer is tagged PROXY and logged in proxy-log.md for review; legal/IP/public/irreversible items are escalated
G4Separate foldersupportedoffice-crawler/ at the repo root
G5Use it to test and improve the harnesssupportedLearnings in docs/harness-learnings.md; fixes go into harness/

  • Not delegated: anything listed under "Never decide" in harness/.claude/agents/customer-proxy.md. Also not delegated: gates of the harness project itself.

hey i missing a place to look at the quest and the next step to solve for them can you put that into the next round after all is done?

Full plan (50-plan.md)

50 Plan

Date: 2026-10-13. Owner: architect. Status: proposed, awaiting plan gate. Inputs: 00-brief.md, 20-requirements.md, 40-nfr.md, circles/circle-01.md (PROXY answers), proxy-log.md, 30-spec/ (files 01-05 and 10 existed when this was written; files for character/skills (R-010..R-016), HUD (R-070..R-077), audio (R-080..R-083), save (R-090..R-092), and the Office theme tone were not yet written, so their work packages cite R-ids and must be re-mapped to AC ids when those files land). Decisions: decisions/ADR-0001-stack.md, ADR-0002-architecture.md, ADR-0003-test-hook.md, ADR-0004-assets.md. Stack pack: static-web (reasons in ADR-0001).

How to read this plan

  • Slices follow the spec: S1 playable core, S2 loot and progression, S3 sound and finale. Each slice ends in a build that can be opened on a preview and demonstrated.
  • A work package (WP) is one implementer run: at most about 600 lines of code (tests excluded from that count but mandatory), one branch/PR, merged in the listed order. Depends names earlier WPs. Packages marked parallel-ok touch disjoint directories.
  • ACs are listed by id from 30-spec/. "Tests" names the files to write; every AC gets a unit test (test/*.test.js) or an E2E check (e2e/*.mjs) as tagged in the spec.
  • Estimates: S = under half a day of agent work, M = about a day, L = more than a day or high uncertainty. Infra changes: only WP S1-1 touches build/CI/preview; migrations: none (no database). Save-format changes in S3 are versioned.
  • Art style is undecided. All WPs that draw things use the Style interface (ADR-0002 section 7). Until the pick, the vector style is the working default (cheapest to produce procedurally); WPs say where a pixel/painterly style becomes a follow-up.

Slice S1: Playable core

Demo at the end of S1 (preview): open the build, click "New game", an isometric office floor appears (open-plan theme), the player walks by clicking, monsters notice and chase, the player fights by clicking them, health and mana gauges update, dying shows a restart control, Esc pauses. ?test=1 exposes the hook and a bot can play it in Node and in the browser.

S1-1 Foundations: skeleton on preview, build hardening, deterministic basics

  • Goal: the pack skeleton is deployed to a preview with a health check; the core's non-negotiable infrastructure exists before any game code (rng with state, clock accumulator, state hash, layering guard, CSP, licence block).
  • Depends: none. Estimate: M. Infra change: yes (preview workflow, build.mjs, CI test step).
  • ACs: AC-R-113-1, AC-R-120-4, AC-NFR-S01-2, AC-NFR-L04-1, AC-NFR-L01-1 (scan harness with the denylist file; list may be empty, QF-10-2), AC-NFR-L01-2, AC-NFR-L05-1 (harness), AC-R-110-3 (title page skeleton has no plug-in elements); health check = page loads with ?test=1 and scene === 'title' (feeds AC-R-110-1).
  • Files: build.mjs (CSP meta, licence block, --style= flag), src/main.js, src/index.html, src/core/clock.js, src/core/hash.js, src/rng.js (add getState/setState, keep the mulberry32 sequence), src/core/config.js (tickHz and first constants), src/core/content/strings.js, src/core/index.js (stub newGame returning {scene:'title'}), .github/workflows/preview.yml from the pack, ASSET-LICENCES.md.
  • Tests: test/rng.test.js + test/fixtures/rng-42.json (golden values recorded once), test/clock.test.js (chunkings), test/hash.test.js (key order independent), test/layering.test.js (no DOM/Date/Math.random/trig in src/core, imports only inward), test/legal.test.js (denylist scans, licence field check, no non-code files in dist), test/build.test.js (CSP tag present, one HTML file), e2e/smoke.mjs updated (title scene, no console error).
  • Risk: low; the preview workflow depends on the pack's [verify] hosting claim. Fallback: serve dist/ statically in CI.

S1-2 Floor model: tiles, generator, path, line of sight, spatial hash, iso math

  • Goal: pure, tested geometry: generate reachable office floors, find paths, project tiles to screen.
  • Depends: S1-1. Parallel-ok with S1-4 start (render shell) after the interfaces in types.js exist. Estimate: L (generator tuning).
  • ACs: AC-R-042-1..-4, AC-R-042-6 (and AC-R-042-5 E2E later), AC-R-003-1 (theme registry open-plan), AC-R-101-1, AC-R-005-8, AC-R-005-9, AC-R-120-3, part of AC-R-112-3 (round trip of tileToScreen/screenToTile), performance AC-R-042-4 (generation time).
  • Files: src/core/tiles.js, grid.js, gen/{floor,rooms,corridors,props,validate}.js, path.js, los.js, spatial.js, content/themes.js (open-plan), content/props.js (office props with blocks), src/render/iso.js.
  • Tests: test/gen.test.js (reachability by flood fill over 200 seeds, entry/exit distance, determinism, different seeds differ, time budget), test/path.test.js (wall-with-gap fixture vs reference BFS, enclosed goal null in under 50 ms on 100x100, corner-cutting rule), test/los.test.js, test/spatial.test.js, test/iso.test.js.
  • Risk: medium: generator quality ("looks like an office") and the retry/fallback guarantee. Mitigation: validation step plus fixed fallback layout; visual quality is reviewed in S1-4.

S1-3 Simulation: player, monsters, melee combat, death

  • Goal: the complete S1 game rules in core, playable headlessly: click-to-move, attack, monsters notice/chase/attack, hit resolution, death/restart, regen, pause.
  • Depends: S1-2. Estimate: L.

Open points and assumptions for the plan gate

  1. Slice tags for character/skills, HUD, audio and save requirements come from files not yet written; the S2/S3 placement above (save and audio in S3, HUD panels and skills in S2) follows the slice names and the S3-tagged ACs seen so far (AC-NFR-O01-1, AC-NFR-Q02-1, AC-NFR-A01-*). Re-map when 06-09 spec files land.
  2. Art style pick must happen before S2-6 at the latest; S1-4 builds the vector style only. A B or C variant needs one WP of its own (about the size of S1-4's style part) if chosen.
  3. Denylists (QF-10-2): the legal scans are meaningless until docs/product/denylist-*.txt exist; WP S1-1 builds the scan harness and fails loudly if a list file is missing.
  4. Playwright is not yet in package.json; WP S1-1 adds it as an exact-version dev dependency (Apache-2.0, allowed by NFR-L04).
  5. Reference runner for performance (QF-10-1): E2E perf assertions are advisory elsewhere.
  6. Spec amendments needed (mechanical): step mutates and returns the same state; alias names added to the hook; decisions table in ADR-0002 section 11 (hit chance, click on wall, skill keys, boss depth, town stairs target, re-entry rules).
  7. Line budget: S1-2, S1-3, S1-4, S2-1..S2-6 and S3-2 are the packages most likely to exceed 600 lines; the implementer should stop at a coherent half and report instead of cramming (split rule: one new WP inserted, same slice).

Rounds R4-R6: classes, skill trees, character selection, five save slots (added 2026-10-14)

Owner: architect. Status: proposed, awaiting plan gate for area M. Inputs: 00-brief.md (Third briefing: "add 3 more rounds of work", 3 classes with skill trees, a visually appealing character-selection screen, 5 save slots in the options menu, keep improving game and tool), 20-requirements.md area M (R-200..R-234), circles/circle-02.md (PROXY answers, binding), decisions/ADR-0005-classes-and-skill-trees.md, decisions/ADR-0006-save-slots.md, ../reviews/R4-contract.md (data contract for the parallel packages, learning L-13).

The customer wrote "3 more rounds of work": one round = one orchestrated cycle (core, then render/UI, then balance and polish), as S1-S3 were. Slices are demoable on a preview: R4 ends with the three classes playable by bot and hook with their trees and five slots working without any new screen; R5 ends with the real screens; R6 ends with parity and polish. Rules from the first plan hold: one WP is one implementer run of at most about 600 lines of code (tests excluded, mandatory), one branch/PR, listed order; if a WP runs over, the implementer stops at a coherent half and reports (split rule: one new WP inserted, same round). Core-first (L-11): bots play all three classes before any sprite exists.

Line counts below are estimates of production code. Estimates S/M/L as above. Infra changes: none. Migrations: save format 1 to 2 (R4-1, R4-5).

Round R8: added item from the seventh briefing (2026-10-14)

R8-1 Follow-ups from the R7 acceptance (docs/reviews/R7-acceptance.md)

  • R8-Q1 (high) bag-full blocks quest gear rewards: reward to the pouch/ground or sell junk from the dialogue.
  • R8-B1 (high) the first floor-1 pack kills level-1 heroes in ~20 s: shrink/split it, check the first 90 s per class.
  • R8-B2 (medium) death spiral at the lift entry (awake monsters near the entry after respawn).
  • R8-B3 (medium) first potions: price vs 50 start gold; bought potions go to the belt.
  • R8-AI1 (medium) deterministic re-click test in a crowd (adjacent attacker hit within 1.5 s).
  • R8-Q2/Q3 (low) close the inventory with the NPC window; second hand-in toast wording.
  • R8-V1 (low) N16 phone map title covered by the dock buttons; N17 elite same size as a manager; N12 tree left gutter.
  • R8-M1 (low, from R7 visual G4) core mapMarkers lists the quest elite and the badge tile once seen; render already draws them.

R8-0 Hero visuals follow equipped gear (customer request, first item of R8)

  • Goal: the hero's figure shows what is equipped in the visible slots (head, body, hands, feet, weapon, off-hand), for all three classes, all facings and animations, in game, on the character sheet and on the character select and slot busts. Rarity reads through colour or trim (Okabe-Ito palette); uniques get a distinct accent.
  • Approach (architect decides in an ADR before work): layered vector parts drawn per item base category (not per item), composited at runtime or cached per equipment combination. Risk: the sprite atlas build is already 4.78 s of a 5 s budget (ADR-0004); pre-baking every combination is not affordable, so the ADR must include an atlas/cache budget.
  • Order: architect ADR + data contract (which item field picks the visual) → WORLD (parts, compositing, cache) with CORE only if a field is missing → UI (sheet/select/busts) → visual review with 1x crops per slot and class → adversarial (every slot × class × facing renders without errors, perf with 50 monsters) → acceptance.

Round R8-T: end-to-end testing and polish (seventh briefing, after R8, before the lighting rounds R9–R10)

  • Goal: a full end-to-end pass over everything built so far: no-cheat full runs per class to the boss in a real browser, save/load across all features (quests, gear visuals, slots), keyboard-only and phone layouts, offline/file:// smoke (incl. write-then-immediate-reload), size, legal and denylist scans, then one polish fix round from the findings.
  • Agents: test-engineer (adversarial, new e2e journeys), reviewer, visual-reviewer, customer-proxy acceptance, retro.

Scope change 2026-10-14 (customer)

R9–R10 (lighting) and R12 (second overall test and polish) are dropped. Order now: R7 (rest) → R8 → R8-T → R11 → end-of-project task.

Files: SESSION-NOTES.md · STATE.md · 50-plan.md

art-direction picked C

What is being decided

Brief: art direction

Question being decided

Which art style should the whole game be built in? The customer wants "nice graphics and sound" and everything generated by us (no external assets, no fonts from CDNs, no image files; see addendum in ../../00-brief.md). The style choice fixes the renderer design, the asset pipeline (all drawn in code), the lighting approach, the HUD look and the effort of every later art task, so it is cheaper to decide now than after the first slice.

Requirements involved

  • R-070 health and mana gauges (here drawn as glass globes with a liquid level; R-070's office-vessel idea, e.g. coffee cup / water jug, is not yet applied)
  • R-071 skill bar (5 icon slots plus one empty slot, XP bar, level)
  • R-112 HTML5 canvas 2D renderer, no plug-ins
  • NFR-A03 colour-blind-safe loot and UI (rarity is shown by colour, marker shape, border style and beam shape)
  • NFR-L01 no third-party names, assets or text (everything on screen is drawn procedurally; names and items are original)
  • NFR performance target: 60 fps on a mid-range laptop (see "Performance" below)
  • Sound (R-080) is not part of this topic; it is a separate synthesis question.

What all three variants share (same content, different style)

Each file is one <canvas> living style tile, animated with requestAnimationFrame:

  • an isometric 2:1 slice of an office level gone wrong: carpet tiles, cubicle partition walls (one collapsed, one doorway), two desks with glowing monitors, a water cooler, a filing cabinet, a hanging fluorescent fixture that flickers and casts a light pool, floor cables, a coffee puddle, stains, scattered paper
  • the hero (office worker, tie, lanyard, keyboard-sword) with a breathing/bob idle and a swing every 2.0 s (wind-up, strike, recover)
  • three monsters: a shambling "Zombie Intern", a hovering "Printer Demon" (paper wings, cable tentacles, orbiting sheets, chomping tray), a hulking "Middle Manager" (elite, binder club)
  • three loot drops, each with a floor ring, light beam, floating label and sparkles: Magic "Sturdy Lanyard of Focus" (blue, diamond marker, plain border, thin beam), Rare "Ergonomic Chair of Haste" (yellow, star marker, double border, wide beam), Unique "The Corner Office Keycard" (orange, hexagon marker, notched double border, widest beam with rising chevrons)
  • a hit effect when the swing lands: flash, damage number, spark and paper-scrap burst, slash arc, target recoil and flash
  • bottom HUD: health and mana globes with an animated liquid surface, skill bar with drawn icons (stapler strike, reply-all, coffee break, mute shield, meeting invite), a cooldown sweep on slot 3, XP bar, level
  • lighting: darkness with a light radius around the hero, the flickering fluorescent pool, monitor glows, cooler, demon and loot glows

How to view

Open A.html, B.html or C.html directly from disk. Everything is inline; no network. ?frame=N renders deterministic frame N (60 frames per second of scene time) and stops animating; this is for screenshots. Good frames: ?frame=92 (just after the hero's hit lands: damage number, particles, flash), ?frame=20 (idle), ?frame=70 (sword raised in wind-up). window.__ready is set after the first frame. The attack loop is 2.0 s; the hit lands at 1.42 s of each cycle.

Common technique (so the comparison is fair)

Same scene description and animation code in all three; only the renderer differs (materials, shading, outlines, lighting, HUD, text). Static geometry (floor, walls, furniture, decals) is drawn once into a cached layer and re-drawn only on resize. Responsive from 390 px wide up; the scene scales with the window and the HUD scales with the viewport height.

Performance

Measured in headless Chromium with software rendering (no GPU, 1440x900, worst case): A and C about 14 ms of frame work, B about 4 ms. With a GPU-backed canvas on a laptop this should be well inside 16 ms, but it has not been measured on real hardware (open question for the Spec phase). B is cheapest because it renders 320x180 pixels and scales the result.

Notes per variant

Notes: art direction variants

How to compare: open the three files at the same window size. Same content, same animation; only the art style changes.

A: Gritty gothic office (A.html)

  • What is different: dark desaturated palette, painterly gradient shading with a thin dark stroke, carpet fibre texture and grime baked into the floor, heavy vignette and real darkness around the hero. Warm candle-like amber monitor light against a sickly green-white fluorescent pool and a red demon glow; additive light bloom, dust motes, serif type, riveted iron-and-glass globes.
  • Suits: the "moody dungeon-crawling" feel of the genre; players who value atmosphere over readability.
  • Trade-offs: hardest to keep readable (dark, low contrast; monsters can sink into the gloom, so gameplay needs rim light or outline helpers); most fill-rate heavy (gradients, additive lights, full-screen darkness layer); every new sprite needs careful shading to avoid looking muddy.
  • Effort for a whole game: L. Many more art decisions per asset, plus lighting performance work and tuning for readability.

B: Crisp pixel art (B.html)

  • What is different: the whole frame is a 320x180 index buffer rasterised by our own code (no canvas antialiasing), 25-colour palette, integer scaling with nearest-neighbour, light falloff by ordered (Bayer) dithering with palette-ramp darkening and warm/cool tints, a built-in 3x5 bitmap font, pixel globes and pixel icons. Rarity uses colour plus marker shape plus border style.
  • Suits: a retro-genre audience, tiny build and runtime budget, very predictable look at any window size (integer scale), easiest to keep consistent.
  • Trade-offs: small sprites limit expression (the hero is about 35 pixels tall); text is blocky and all caps; portrait phones get a small crisp image with margins, not a larger crop; hand-tuning of sprites will eventually beat the procedural primitives used in this tile (it needs a pixel-sprite pipeline: either hand-written sprite arrays or a small procedural pixel-drawing library).
  • Effort for a whole game: M. The rendering is cheap and consistent, but sprite animation frames and the palette discipline need steady care.

C: Stylised vector (C.html)

  • What is different: bold dark outlines, flat colours with one shade step per surface, rim light on up-left edges, oversized heads and cartoony proportions, banded (toon) lighting instead of smooth gradients, saturated accents on a dark indigo base, flat glossy globes, rounded sans-serif UI with outlined text.
  • Suits: best readability at a glance (silhouettes, rarity and enemies pop), friendly and humorous office tone, scales to any resolution without blur, easiest style to extend with new monsters and items because shapes are built from a few primitives.
  • Trade-offs: least "dark dungeon" atmosphere of the three (the tone is darker than it first looks, but moodiness comes from colour, not light); outlines cost fill-rate; risks looking generic unless the palette and proportions are kept distinctive.
  • Effort for a whole game: M. New assets are cheap; the cost is keeping outline width, shade rules and rim-light rules consistent.

Cross-cutting findings

  • All three met the stated constraints: single file, no external assets or fonts, drawn in code, original names, 390 px wide up, ?frame=N, window.__ready.
  • File sizes: A about 49 KB, B about 44 KB, C about 47 KB (the harness rule of ~60 KB is met).
  • All three share one scene engine (scene description, animation, hit effect, lighting inputs). A real game would keep that split: a style-independent scene and a swappable renderer. That makes a later style change (or a high-contrast accessibility mode) cheaper.
  • Performance is likely fine for all three on a laptop with a GPU-backed canvas, but only measured in software rendering (see brief.md). A and C each use two half-resolution light layers composed once per frame; the full game needs a test with 50 monsters (NFR).
  • Not covered: sound, character art beyond the one hero, tile variety, fonts for localisation, large-screen performance at 4K.

C2: stylised vector, round 2 (C2.html)

Copy of C with the combined round-1 review fixes (review-r1-appeal.md, review-r1-craft.md). A, B, C and decision.md are unchanged.

  • Tone: world graded dark with A's lighting model. One baked mask holds a 90 % darkness layer, a toon-banded hero-radius light, a heavier vignette, and coloured pools (cold fluorescent, cyan monitor glow, red emergency lamp and demon glow, loot glow). Blood decals, wall smears and tile scuffs added. Outlines, flat colours and silhouettes are kept.
  • Readability: each actor gets a 2 px rim ring drawn from a silhouette pass under the normal pass (hero near-white, zombie lime, demon red, manager amber). Hero is bigger (+10 %), brightest and warmest (white shirt, royal-blue suit, yellow tie, cyan lanyard); the zombie is a darker, ragged green. Loot labels are about 60 % of nameplate size (serif italic for Unique) and are placed once per layout by a small collision pass against actors, nameplates, the damage-number zone and the HUD, with a leader line when displaced. The damage number drifts up-right, and the Zombie nameplate sits under its feet.
  • Rarity (NFR-A03): Okabe-Ito sky blue / yellow / vermillion. Simulated deuteranopia: Rare-vs-Unique colour difference dE 30 (C: 18), lightness 90 vs 61; protanopia dE 49 (C: 30). Markers (diamond, star, hexagon), border styles (plain, double, notched with white inner line) and beam shapes are kept.
  • HUD: health is a coffee mug with a heart glyph and bubbles, mana is a water-cooler jug with a drop glyph and ripples; both show current/max. XP bar shows LEVEL 7 and 38% to level 8; skill bar has key badges outside the icon area, names under the icons (desktop), and a cooldown number.
  • Phone (390 and 360 px): all 6 slots, full-width skill bar, globes above the bar corners, labels clamped 8 px inside the viewport, no horizontal scroll. The scene is cropped to the action, which leaves empty dark area above it on tall phones (deliberate; no extra tiles drawn).
  • Performance: world, light mask and HUD frame are baked per layout; labels and nameplates are pre-rendered sprites; only the fluorescent flicker, actors, liquid, effects and the cooldown are drawn per frame. Measured in headless Chromium software GL, 1280x800: C2 about 54 fps (range 45 to 60 over repeated runs), C 27 to 30 fps in the same run. Still a pessimistic number, not real hardware.
  • Trade-offs: actors are drawn after the darkness (self-lit, with only a small dimming for the far ones), so they do not receive the coloured pools; the look is "cel-lit" rather than physically lit. Each actor is drawn twice (ring + body), which is the main per-frame cost (about 8 fps) and the thing to watch with 50 monsters; a sprite cache per monster type would remove it. File size 58 KB (limit about 60 KB).
  • Effort for a whole game: M, unchanged from C; the lighting bake and the placement pass are reusable engine parts.

C3: stylised vector, round 3 "more detail and polish" (C3.html)

Answers the real customer's fifth briefing ("idea is good but more details and polishing", 2026-10-14). C2 stays the frozen identity (bold outlines, readable silhouettes, dark grade, Okabe-Ito rarity, same actors, loot, hit FX and HUD layout); C3 adds a detail layer on top. Switches: ?scene=office|basement|boardroom, ?frame=N (+ window.__ready), ?compare=1 (C2 | C3 wipe, draggable divider or the range input, &split=NN), ?legacy=1 (every round-3 addition off, matches C2 pixel for pixel apart from 6 e-5 of the pixels; it is what the compare view uses for the left half), ?zoom=3&focus=hero|zom|dem|mgr (review aid, hides labels). What read as flat or bare in the current game shots (final-lobby, polish-basement, s3-boss-phase2, final-champion-fight, final-inventory-compare): one repeated floor diamond with no tile-to-tile variation; wall panels as flat slabs with only a small framed picture; grey cabinets and desks with no material feel; props sparse and floating (no contact shadow or occlusion at wall bases); hero and monsters single-tone cel with no cloth, face or secondary motion; HUD panels flat purple with no depth.

What changed, and what each costs when ported to the game engine (S/M/L = small/medium/large, against the C2 renderer):

  1. Baked material textures (carpet plain/twill/basket weave with mirrored tile orientation and per-tile tone drift, wood grain, brushed metal, concrete, plaster, wall panel, paper, cardboard): 11 procedural 64x64 alpha overlays, created once into offscreen canvases and applied as createPattern fills with a skew matrix per face type (top, left, right). Per-frame cost 0 (static layer). Port: S, one texture(name) + patternFor(face) helper, material table maps material to texture.
  2. Second shade level + ambient occlusion: every static vertical face gets a base-darkening gradient on top of the existing flat shade steps; floor gets wall-base AO strips and soft contact shadows (four stacked rounded rects) under every prop; bevelled tile seams (dark joint, lit up-left edge). Baked. Port: S for the gradient, S for contact shadows if props already have footprints.
  3. Light spill and pools: extra baked pools in the existing light mask (second fixture pool, monitor floor spill, desk-lamp pool, green exit-sign pool, window light shaft across the floor, a brighter inner band on fixture pools); screens spill a cyan glow onto the desk (additive, per frame, 2 sprites). Cost: M-/S (more entries in the same bake; the dynamic part is 2 additive draws). Port: S, the bake already exists.
  4. Density (office): a second fixture, door ajar, door mat, runner carpet with stitch lines, hazard tape, painted chevrons, footprints from the door, coffee rings, scuffs, cable tape wraps, plants, bin with paper, wet-floor A-frame sign, box stack, extinguisher, desk lamp, mugs, sticky notes, keyboard keys, filing-cabinet drawers with labels, glass partition panes, skirting boards, sockets, vents, wall clock, framed chart, three humour posters, cork board with notices and sticky notes, whiteboard, a skyline window with reflections, exit sign. All static. Port: M. This is content, not engine: a prop kit of about 40 sprites or draw functions plus a decal/wall-item placement list per room. Wall items draw in a small "wall space" transform (1 unit = 1 design px), which is the reusable piece (S).
  5. Two more scenes from the same engine and actors: basement (concrete, cracked and stained, safe-lane paint, drain, puddles with glint, pipe runs, server racks with blinking LEDs, filing cabinets, shelving, boiler, barrels, caged bulbs, breaker panel, signage) and boardroom (burgundy lattice carpet with gold inlay and a bordered rug, panelled walls, glass-topped table with laptops, high-back chairs, credenza with trophies, projector slide, framed founders, curtained windows, chandeliers). Port: M each (content) on top of the shared S engine work; a per-scene table holds palette overrides, textures, fixtures and light list.
  6. Characters: hero gets eyebrow, nose, smile, blush, lens glint, hair highlight strands and cowlick, headset band and boom, collar, lapel notches, pocket square, tie stripes, belt buckle, cuffs, trouser creases, shoe laces and soles, badge photo; zombie gets tears, stitches, eye bags, fangs, drool, skin mottling; manager gets nose, stubble, comb-over strands, sweat drop, pinstripes, buttons, folds, belt buckle, sticky note on the binder; the printer demon gets a control panel (flickering LCD, buttons, blinking LED), vents and CMY toner stripes. Detail is skipped in the silhouette (rim) pass. Secondary motion: tie sway (hero, zombie, manager), cowlick and zombie hair-tuft bob, comb-over sway and sweat drip, LCD flicker, monitor scan band and glitch rows, rack LEDs. Cost: about +2 ms per frame for four actors (see below). Port: M, and the right place to cache: per-monster-type sprite caches of the static detail with only the swaying parts drawn live (that was already the recommended fix for 50 monsters, and it now matters a little more).
  7. Outline weight is clamped (clamp(2.0*zoom, 1.6, 4.2) px) instead of growing linearly, so at game scale (hero about 100 px) the line stays about 2.4 px and does not get heavier on big screens. Port: S.
  8. UI chrome: panel with top-to-bottom sheen, brushed-metal grain, inner shadow, top bevel and a stitched dashed border; skill slots with inner shadow, bottom light, corner rivets; XP bar with inner shadow and divider; mug with glaze gradient, stitched bands, speckle, rivets; jug with ribbed plastic, rivets, brushed rim; icons snapped to whole pixels, with drop shadow and a specular stroke. Baked once per layout, 0 per frame. Port: S (needs the HUD bake that C2 already has).
  9. Ambient motion: dust motes drifting and twinkling inside fixture and hero pools (about 40 tiny additive dots per frame), a second fluorescent with its own flicker pattern, cage-bulb and chandelier glow, blinking rack LEDs. Cost S.
  10. Performance (headless Chromium, software GL, 1280x800; compositor-capped at 60): C3 office 58, basement 59, boardroom 60 fps; C2 60 fps on the same machine. Render cost per frame including a forced flush: C2 11.7 ms, C3 office 13.5 ms, basement 13.8 ms, boardroom 12.3 ms (so about 74 fps uncapped for C3, against about 85 for C2). Layout/bake on resize: C2 9 ms, C3 14 to 15 ms (textures are built once, patterns re-created per zoom); not per frame.
  11. File size: 124 KB, over the ~60 KB guideline for variant files, because it carries three scenes, the texture generators, the compare view and a legacy path. It is a style reference, not a product file; the port does not carry the legacy path or the compare view.
  12. Checks: single self-contained file, no network references (no urls, fetch, link or script src), no ip-denylist terms, no console errors, window.__ready set (compare mode sets it when both iframes report ready), phone width 390 renders without horizontal scroll. The compare view loads this same file twice in iframes (?legacy=1 and normal).
  13. Trade-offs and risks: (a) the grade is still dark, so floor weave and wall materials show mostly inside light pools; a brighter ambient floor is a one-number change but would dilute the C2 mood; (b) actors are still drawn after the darkness and do not receive pool colour, so monsters can look a touch "pasted on" next to the richer floors; (c) the humour posters and signs are tiny text that is readable at 1280x800 but not at game scale: they are texture, not copy to localise; (d) the basement wall pipes are busy behind the racks; (e) review at 100% size, the compare divider cuts through the hero at the default 50% split (use &split=30 or drag).
  14. Screenshots: shots/r3/C3-default-f92.jpg, C3-basement-f92.jpg, C3-boardroom-f92.jpg, C3-compare-f92.jpg.
Decision

Decision: art direction

Status: decided (PROXY), style frozen after round-2 review (appeal 33 ship, craft 32 ship) Date: 2026-10-13 Picked: C (stylised vector), graded darker with A's lighting model ("C-dark") Confidence: medium (high that C is the right base; medium on how dark the grade goes)

PROXY decision, provisional until the real customer reviews it. Overrule any part in proxy-log.md.

Reasons

  1. Customer words: "we want nice sound and graphics" and "stay close to the original" (00-brief.md: close in mechanics and feel; original art is not to be copied). "Nice graphics" is met by C most clearly: both reviewers scored it highest (appeal 34/40, craft 30/40, A 31/29, B 27/26) and both ranked C > A > B. Viewed C-desk-f92 myself: the hit moment (outlined "63", paper burst, recoil) and the silhouettes read at a glance.
  2. "Feel of the original" is a hack-and-slash that must be played for hours. That depends on readability in crowds (up to 50 monsters, NFR-P01), where C is best and A is worst (dark-on-dark actors, 23 fps software GL). A is the mood reference, not a base.
  3. Moodiness is the one thing C lacks (theme 3/5 in both reviews), but it is a grade, not a redraw: both reviewers say it can be bought back with value, vignette and light. A's mood is expensive to get right at scale (effort L); C's is cheap to fix (effort M).
  4. B: cheapest and most consistent, but the 35 px actors cannot carry ten monsters and a boss, and the phone view is unusable. Lowest appeal.
  5. Risk on record: if the real customer values "moody" over "friendly and readable", A (with its readability and performance budget) is the alternative. This is a taste call within delegated scope (Q2 look and tone); nothing legal or irreversible. Not an IP question: all three are original drawn art.

Art-direction rules (what to borrow)

Primary style: C. Bold dark outlines at constant screen width, flat fills with one shade step per surface, rim light on up-left edges, banded light.

From A (tone and light):

  • Grade the floor and wall values about 25% darker than r1 C, with a strong vignette and real darkness outside the hero's light radius; keep outlines and flat colours.
  • Light model: warm amber monitor pools, a cold green-white flickering fluorescent pool with a clear edge, a red emergency tint on the demon side. Implement as a pre-baked low-resolution light mask plus sprite-level glow, max 4 dynamic lights.
  • A few grime / stain / blood decals on floor and cubicle walls (baked into the static layer).
  • Replace C's purple globe rim with a riveted iron-and-glass frame.
  • Serif or slab type for Unique item names only; sans stays for all other UI.
  • Keep the floor-to-wall value separation at least 3:1 inside the hero's radius so the layout still reads after darkening.

From B (discipline and performance):

  • One palette, one outline weight, pixel-snapped HUD. Cache all sprites and static geometry in offscreen canvases; light layers at half resolution or lower.
  • A quality switch ("low fx": dithered or flat darkening instead of blended light) targeting 40+ fps in software GL; this doubles as the high-contrast/low-fx option.
  • Keep the shared scene engine separate from a swappable renderer (notes.md cross-cutting finding).

Shared rules for all later art: rarity is never colour alone (marker shape, border style, beam shape, which C already does); rim light on every actor so none sinks into the dark; label text sizes are demoted relative to characters.

Must-fix items for the next round (both reviews)

Readability and feedback

  1. Damage number spawns above the target's nameplate and head and rises over about 400 ms; the nameplate fades during the hit. It must never cover the Zombie Intern plate or the hero's face (C-desk-f92).
  2. Hero must separate from the Zombie Intern: hero about 10% larger, bright lanyard/tie highlight, distinct face value (not the Manager's skin value); zombie darker green with a ragged silhouette.
  3. Reduce label clutter: loot plates smaller (about 60%), full text on hover/Alt or when the hero is near, nameplates directly above each head; no label may overlap another or the fluorescent fixture.
  4. Manager's oversized head must read as attached to the body (shoulders/neck or a size change).

Tone

  1. Darker grade, stronger vignette, dark falloff outside the hero's light, cold green fluorescent pool with a clear edge, red emergency tint near the demon, grime decals (see rules above). Re-test readability after grading.

Accessibility (NFR-A03/A04)

  1. Health and mana distinguishable without hue: numeric value in or under each globe, a glyph per globe (heart/flame or similar), and different liquid-surface patterns. Test with deuteranopia and protanopia filters.
  2. Rare vs Unique: separate further than yellow vs orange: Rare toward lighter lime-gold, Unique deep orange-red with a notched border and white inner stroke; markers at least 16 px; keep the shape and beam differences. Test with a colour-blind filter.
  3. High-contrast option noted for later (body text 4.5:1 on all label plates).

Layout and polish

  1. Clamp all labels to a safe area (8 px from the edge) and shorten nameplates on narrow screens; show all 6 skill slots (or scroll). Phone is secondary (NFR-B02: MVP minimum 1024 px), so this is lightly weighted but the clamp is cheap.
  2. Skill bar: slot number must not overlap icon corners; simplify busy icons 2 and 5 at 70 px.

Performance

  1. Cache sprites to offscreen canvases and bake outlines; light layers at reduced resolution; re-measure and report at least 40 fps in software GL (r1: 29), with a test scene of 50 monsters before committing to the renderer design.

Risk to watch

  1. C looking generic: keep the distinctive palette (indigo base, teal walls, warm accents) and the office-comedy proportions; the reviewers should check distinctiveness in round 2.

Next

One round-2 pass of C-dark on the same tile (fixes 1 to 12), reviewed by both visual reviewers, then freeze the style. No new variants.

Round G (C3): graphics detail round

Date: 2026-10-14 Status: decided (PROXY) Confidence: high on direction (port, no mock-up); medium on the exact lift (12 %)

PROXY decision, provisional until the real customer reviews it. Overrule any part in proxy-log.md. Input: fifth briefing (verbatim, 00-brief.md): "the style idea is good but more details and polishing" (real customer, agreed). Reviews: appeal C2 28 / C3 31, craft C2 29 / C3 31, both "iterate". Viewed C3-default-f92 and C3-boardroom-f92 myself.

Decision on the orchestrator's proposal: APPROVED, with two adjustments

  • No C4 mock-up round. The customer said the style idea is good; the style is frozen and the reviews give a concrete port list. Port straight into the game, then review in-game at real scale (hero about 100 to 135 px), not at the 200 px of the mock-up. A further mock-up would only re-argue a settled style.
  • Adjustment 1: the in-game review is the gate. Both reviewers re-score in the game with the same 8 criteria; target 34+ (appeal reviewer's estimate with items 1 to 5). If under 33, one more fix pass, still no new variants.
  • Adjustment 2: every item below is checked at game scale; anything under about 2 px that does not read at 1x is dropped, not ported "for later".

Mood question: LIFT, +12 % ambient mid-tone outside the light pools

Reasons:

  1. The customer asked for "more details"; both reviewers independently found the dark grade hides the new materials (floor weave, wall panels, bevels) everywhere except inside pools. Detail the player cannot see does not answer the brief.
  2. "Stay close to the original" is about mechanics and feel (brief); the moody read comes from pools, vignette, coloured light and contrast between lit and unlit, not from near-black corners. A modest lift keeps all of that.
  3. Round-1 decision (C-dark) already made the grade darker with medium confidence; this is a refinement within the same Q2 call, not a reversal. The boardroom shot already shows that materials plus dark mood work together.

Limits (keep the mood):

  • Lift only the ambient floor/wall mid-tones, about +12 % luminance (allowed range 10 to 15 %). Do NOT lift the vignette corners or the pool-to-ambient ratio: pools must stay clearly brighter and more saturated. The darkest 15 % of the frame stays dark.
  • Prefer hue shift per tile (warm/cool alternate) and texture alpha 1.5x inside pools over pure brightness, so the lift can stay small.
  • Make it one named constant (AMBIENT_LIFT) so the real customer can turn it back to 0 in one edit. Record the before/after screenshots.
  • Floor-to-wall separation stays at least 3:1 inside the hero's radius (round-1 rule).

This is an identity call; flagged for the real customer in proxy-log.md to confirm or revert.

Merged port checklist (WORLD implementer; order matters)

Port as is (baked, 0 per frame)

  1. Outline clamp clamp(2.0*zoom, 1.6, 4.2).
  2. Contact shadows under props and wall-base AO strips in the static bake.
  3. Bevelled tile seams plus per-tile tone drift and mirrored orientation (breaks the repeated diamond).
  4. HUD chrome bake: panel sheen, inner shadow, stitched border, rivets, mug and jug glaze, snapped icons.
  5. Extra baked light pools, second fixture, window light shaft, exit-sign pool, brighter inner band; max 4 dynamic lights still holds.
  6. Basement and boardroom scene tables (palette, textures, fixtures, lights) on the shared engine; boardroom lattice carpet as is.
  7. Baked material textures (11 procedural 64x64 overlays, patterns re-created only on zoom change).

Amplify so it reads at 1x

  1. AMBIENT_LIFT +12 % (above), hue-shifted tiles, texture alpha 1.5x inside pools (light mask above about 40 %).
  2. Actors receive pool colour: multiply tint 15 to 25 % from the light colour at the feet plus a soft coloured ground shadow (both reviewers' top gap).
  3. Characters: 2-tone shading (light/shadow side) and 2 to 3 large colour blocks per type (hero white shirt panel, cyan lanyard, contrasting shoes; zombie torn sleeve in a second green, grey-purple trousers; manager lighter lapel); faces 1.5x larger and darker; detail strokes at least 1.5 px at zoom 1.8. Keep hero headset, tie stripes, badge; zombie crown tuft, torn hem, one big mouth with two fangs; demon CMY stripes and LCD; manager pinstripes, buttons, brow and mouth bar.
  4. Props: 3 to 4 distinctive large silhouettes per room kind at about 40 to 70 px (office: coffee machine, water cooler, plant, copier; basement: barrel, valve wheel, pallet; boardroom: podium, trophy case); top face or outline one value step lighter; rim-light 1 px edges on wall tops, desk and table edges facing light; per-area wall-base glow (teal / rust / burgundy). Props and floor paint never overlap loot spawn zones.
  5. Secondary motion that reads at 1x: tie sway 2 to 3x, 2 px idle breathing bob on hero and manager, visible mug steam; live-draw only the swaying parts over a per-type cached sprite.
  6. Cache first: per-monster-type sprite cache of static detail before any live detail; budget atlas bake at most 5 s, fps50 p50 at least 40 with 50 monsters.

Drop (do not port)

  1. Posters, cork-board notices, framed-chart text, signs and the wall-space transform (unless needed for window/board panels).
  2. Manager stubble, sweat drip, comb-over strands, nose; zombie tears, eye bags, mottling, drool; hero laces, trouser creases, cuffs.
  3. Dust motes (keep only if fps50 has slack after item 12), second flicker pattern, LCD flicker.
  4. White fixture glint slashes (drop or tone to about 40 %, they out-shout loot labels).
  5. Fine pixel decals: door mat, coffee rings, footprints, cable tape, scuffs, sockets, vents, keyboard keys, drawer labels. Keep 3 to 4 larger decal types.
  6. Yellow safe-lane colour: ochre, outside the loot band, never near the yellow rarity colour.
  7. Legacy switch, compare view, zoom aid, inlined three-scene generator file.

Acceptance: every must-fix of round 1 still holds (no label covers the damage number, hero separates from zombie, rarity not by colour alone), then in-game review by both visual reviewers.

To pick: tell Claude "pick art-direction variant X because …", or edit variants/art-direction/decision.md.

character-select picked A

What is being decided

Character selection screen: variants

Date: 2026-10-14. Topic character-select. Maker: prototyper.

Question being decided

The real customer asked for "a visually appealing character selection screen" (third briefing, ../../00-brief.md). How should the player meet the three classes and choose one: where does the character stand, how does the stage relate to the information, and how does it fit on a phone? Circle 2 (../../circles/circle-02.md) answered class concepts; the names below are working names and the final names stay escalated (R-233).

Requirements involved

R-200 (three classes), R-202 (a skill tree per class), R-210 / R-211 (name and class, name rules 1 to 16 characters), R-212 (visually appealing, intent), R-213 (selection screen content), R-214 (keyboard, accessibility, performance), R-215 (flow title, slot, class, game), R-220 / R-222 / R-223 (five slots, slot preview, reachable from the screen), NFR-A07, NFR-P06.

What all three variants share

  • Same content: class name, one-line pitch, playstyle tags, four stat bars (Toughness, Damage, Speed, Reach, 1 to 5 plus the number, so not colour-only), difficulty (text plus three dots), the three skill-branch names with an icon each (branch names from circle 2), a name field (label, 1 to 16 characters with counter, Suggest button), Start, and Load game.
  • Load game opens a dialog with the 5 slots (sample data: four filled, slot 5 empty; class, level, depth, play time, last played; class bust on each). Empty slot offers "New game here". Start shows which slot a new game will use.
  • Frozen art style (C2): flat fill plus one shade, bold dark outline, one rim-light arc, oversized head. Three figures drawn on canvas, each with an idle loop and a 1.7 s "selected" flourish: Facilities Manager (wrench slam and shockwave), Sales Rep (fan of business cards and a stapler), IT Wizard (Reboot: spell circle, power glyph, flying keycaps).
  • Input: mouse (click a class, buttons), keyboard (Left/Right or A/D, 1/2/3, Enter replays the flourish, L opens Load, N or / jumps to the name field, Esc closes the dialog, Tab order sane, visible focus ring), radiogroup semantics for the class choice. prefers-reduced-motion freezes idle and flourish.
  • Screenshot hooks: ?frame=N (deterministic, N frames at 60 fps, no animation loop), ?sel=0|1|2, window.__ready. Extras: ?name=... prefills the name, ?load=1 opens the slot dialog.
  • Single file, no external requests, each about 43 to 46 KB. Dark theme only (the game is dark); contrast checked by eye on the rendered shots, not measured.

Not in these variants

Name collision or profanity rules, overwrite and delete confirmations (R-221), the tree panel itself (only branch names and icons), sound, and any final class names or game title.

Files

A.html, B.html, C.html, notes.md, decision.md, shots/ (two JPEGs per variant), figures.js (the exported figure functions, identical to the marked FIGURES section in each HTML).

Notes per variant

Notes per variant

A. Lobby lineup

  • Three characters stand in the dimly lit Lobby; the chosen one steps forward (down and larger) into a ceiling-lamp cone and a banded light pool with a white selection ring, like the in-game selection ring. Info panel is a fixed column on the right (stacked above the form on a phone).
  • Suits: players who want to compare the three bodies side by side and feel "the world"; best match to the in-game look (docs/shots/final-lobby.jpg) so the figures can later be reused as in-world sprites. Trade-off: the unchosen two are dimmed, so their pose detail is less visible; labels are small chips on the floor.
  • Effort: M (one canvas scene, DOM panel). Closest to what the WORLD renderer already does; lowest risk for performance (one canvas, three figures).

B. Personnel files

  • Three manila folders with ID badges fan out on a wooden desk; choosing one lifts it and opens a paper "file" with a polaroid of the character (full figure plays the flourish, a SELECTED stamp slams down), stat form, branches and the name line. Paper theme (dark ink on cream), typewriter labels.
  • Suits: the customer who wants the office joke front and centre, and the most phone-friendly layout (photo becomes a banner, folders fan across the top). Trade-off: the characters appear small (badge busts and one photo), only one is shown full-length at a time, and the paper look departs from the dark game UI; the name field doubles as a form line.
  • Effort: M (DOM and CSS carry most of it; four small canvases). The desk props are static art that need redrawing if the style shifts.

C. Elevator doors

  • Each class waits in its own elevator car. Choosing a car opens its doors with a bright light, a floor spill and a "ding" flash on the indicator; the figure plays the flourish inside while the other doors stay shut with a thin light seam. Stats sit below in three columns.
  • Suits: the most dramatic reveal and the clearest "one at a time" focus; fits the game's elevator descent. Trade-off: closed cars hide the other two classes completely (the player must open a car to see who is inside), the stage is the least dense, and the figure is clipped to the door frame, which limits big flourish effects. Needs a short wait (about 1 s) for the doors on each change.
  • Effort: M. Door animation is simple, but the light and the clipping need care for each new effect; the three-column stats area needs the most responsive work.

Shared figure code

The three class figures are one section in each file marked FIGURES (exported, port to src/render/styles) and also saved as figures.js. API: drawFacilitiesManager(ctx,t,f,dim), drawSalesRep(...), drawITWizard(...), drawClassFigure(i,...). The context must be translated to the feet and scaled (the figure is about 97 units tall, y up is negative); t is idle seconds, f is the flourish 0..1 or -1, dim darkens toward a silhouette. The figures use their own small helpers (fE, fP, fL, fGlow, fText, fmix) and a palette FIG_MATS, so they can be lifted without the screen code. They are drawn front-on, not in the game's isometric view; the WORLD implementer will need isometric or three-quarter variants for in-world sprites, but the proportions, palette and props carry over.

Answers (customer-proxy, 2026-10-14)

  1. Variant or mix: PROXY (confidence high): A "Lobby lineup", with borrowings from C and B (see decision.md). Basis: customer asked for "visually appealing"; reviewer scored A 34/40 vs 30 and 28, and A matches the game's look.
  2. Unchosen classes visible: PROXY (confidence high): yes, all three stay visible (A). Basis: comparing classes is the point of a class screen; genre convention is a visible lineup; C hides two of three.
  3. Dark vs paper look: PROXY (confidence high): dark, matching the game. Paper look only as small accents (stamp, badge bust). Basis: customer wants a coherent game ("nice graphics"); reviewer cohesion score B=2.
  4. Class, stat and difficulty names: PROXY (confidence medium): working names proceed (Facilities Manager / Sales Rep / IT Wizard; Toughness, Damage, Speed, Reach). ESCALATE: final names are a brand decision for the real customer (R-233).
Decision

Decision: character selection screen

Status: decided (PROXY) Date: 2026-10-14 Picked: A "Lobby lineup" Confidence: high for A over B and C; medium for the borrow list Decided by: customer-proxy, provisional until the real customer reviews. Logged in ../../proxy-log.md.

Basis: customer words "a visually appealing character selection screen" and "stay close to the original" (../../00-brief.md); review-r1.md (A 34/40, ship-range; C 30; B 28); I looked at all six screenshots in shots/.

Reasons

  • Most appealing on sight: a lit lobby with three full-length characters, the chosen one stepping into a light cone and ring. The unchosen classes stay visible, so the player can compare.
  • Same dark look and selection ring as the game, so the figures can become in-world sprites. B's cream paper screen breaks the dark UI and its folders cut off the names. C hides two of the three classes and clips the best flourish.
  • Best phone layout (fits at 390x844 without scroll) and lowest effort and risk (one canvas).

Answers to the open questions

  1. Variant: A, with borrowings below.
  2. Unchosen classes: visible.
  3. Look: dark game look. Paper only as accents.
  4. Class, stat and difficulty names stay working names. ESCALATE: needs the real customer for final names (R-233).

Borrow rules

  • From C: the three-column stats row below the stage as the layout for short or landscape-phone windows; a short "ding" pulse on the selection ring when switching class; the elevator doors as the transition after Start (figure walks in, doors close). Optional, only if room.
  • From B: the SELECTED stamp as the confirmation beat after Start; the ID-badge bust as the class card in the Load dialog and a future File screen; the "CONFIDENTIAL, FLOOR 0" micro-copy.
  • From all: keep the shared 5-slot Load dialog and the text-plus-number stat bars. Do not borrow B's paper theme or C's blind doors.

Must-fix list (before this screen is accepted)

Reviewer's top 5 for A:

  1. Re-space the stage (about 22 / 50 / 78 percent of the width) so the forward-stepped figure, ring and cone are never cut at the edge; keep the cone inside the stage.
  2. Make the unchosen two readable: dim no lower than about 70 percent brightness, keep a 1 px rim light and their props (stapler, laptop edge), add a hover lift; move class chips closer to the feet and enlarge them.
  3. Fill the info panel's dead zone (emblem or portrait plus a one-line playstyle quote) or enlarge the name field and make Start the brightest object.
  4. Fix Start's disabled state: class accent at about 40 percent, a visible hint "Type a name to start", text contrast at least 4.5:1.
  5. Keyboard and phone: restore focus to "Load game" on Esc or Close; sticky header and Close in the phone dialog; phone class chips at least 44 px high; a "most recent" tag in the slot list.

Also from the review: readable stapler against the floor, legible keycap labels (or no labels at small sizes), simpler Facilities face at bust size.

Figures feedback (customer-facing priority): the in-world hero is currently a plain blue-shirted worker, so players would not recognise their class when the game starts. The in-world class sprites must carry each class's identity from the selection screen:

  • Facilities Manager: yellow hard hat and hi-vis vest (orange accent), wrench.
  • Sales Rep: suit and headset (pink accent), business cards or stapler.
  • IT Wizard: hoodie and laptop (cyan accent), keycap or glow accent.

Keep the C2 style, silhouettes and palette from figures.js; draw isometric or three-quarter variants at in-world size; add a check that the three sprites are distinguishable at about 60 px.

Escalations

  • Final class names, stat names and game title (brand, R-233). Working names proceed.

inventory-panel picked C

What is being decided

Brief: inventory panel, equipment and Employee File (slice S2)

Question being decided

How should the in-game inventory/equipment panel and the character sheet be laid out and opened? S2 adds items, equipment, attributes and levelling, so the player will open these panels constantly. The choice sets how much of the play area stays visible, how fast items can be compared and swapped, and what the phone view looks like.

Requirements involved

  • R-050..R-053, R-055 items, rarity, affixes, equipment slots (ten slots: head, ID badge/amulet, body, gloves, shoes, belt, weapon, off-hand, 2 rings), 10x4 grid with items from 1x1 to 2x4
  • R-054 requirements (level, attribute); no durability (Q3)
  • R-056 potion belt on keys 1-4 (potions never share keys with skills; skills are F1-F4 plus right mouse, QF-01-4)
  • R-057 gold shown with the inventory
  • R-061 hover tooltip with comparison to the equipped item (numeric difference per stat)
  • R-011, R-012, R-016 attributes, derived stats, stat-point allocation, preview of what the next point does, items whose requirements are not yet met
  • R-072, R-073 character panel (key C) and inventory panel (key I)
  • R-051-2, NFR-A03 rarity never by colour alone (mark shape + border pattern + word + colour); NFR-A04 text contrast >= 4.5:1
  • R-102, R-103 original office-themed names (no names from the genre original)

Fixed by the frozen art direction (C2) and shared by all three variants

  • C2 palette: dark purple plates with thick near-black outlines and an inner rim line, Okabe-Ito rarity colours (sky blue magic, yellow rare, vermillion unique), Trebuchet-style sans, the coffee-mug health and water-jug mana vessels and the bottom bar (skill slots F1-F4, belt 1-4) as in the ported game shot.
  • Office re-expression: character sheet = "Employee File" (paper sheet with a probation stamp), inventory = "Desk Drawer", amulet slot = "ID badge", gloves, shoes, belt. Gold is plain "gold".
  • Same 19 synthetic items (12 in the drawer, 5 equipped, 2 potions on the belt): normal / magic / rare / unique, original pun names and plausible affixes. Comparison cases: Reorg Letter Opener (rare weapon) is better than the equipped Ergonomic Keyboard of Haste; Threadbare Hi-Vis Vest is worse than the equipped Pinstripe Blazer; The Corner Office Keycard (unique) is better but needs level 8 (player is 7, so it is marked unmet); Fingerless Gloves of Dexterity need Agility 10 (player has 9, one stat point unlocks them). A two-handed Splintered Chair Leg shows the off-hand rule (QF-05-4).
  • Interaction (simulated, no backend): I and C open/close, Esc closes or puts a held item back, drag and drop or click-then-click, swap on overlap with one item, rejection with a message otherwise (does not fit, overlaps two items, wrong slot, requirement not met), potion keys 1-4 (potion consumed, health/mana vessel moves), "+" on an attribute (spends a point, derived stats update, previewed on hover/focus).
  • Keyboard: Tab to slots and belt, arrow keys inside the grid (one tab stop), Enter/Space picks up and places, tooltips show on focus, visible focus ring, live region announces results.
  • Rarity key (mark, border style, name) is shown inside the inventory panel. Text contrast was measured in the browser for all visible text in both desktop and phone layouts (no pair below 4.5:1).
  • Test hooks: window.__ready = true after render; ?open=inv|char|both; ?hover=<itemId> (item ids: kbd, blazer, lanyard, signet, loafers, opener, vest, keycard, headset, gloves, cinch, overtime, clipboard, chairleg, staples, coffee, energy).
  • Each file is one self-contained HTML (about 53-56 KB), no external requests. The game view behind is a static dimmed canvas drawing, not the real renderer.

Files

A.html, B.html, C.html, notes.md, decision.md, shots/ (1280x800 compare shot and 390x844 shot per variant; B's phone shot shows the Employee File tab).

Notes per variant

Notes: inventory panel variants

A Classic split

  • Employee File (left half) and Desk Drawer (right half) both open together, like the genre convention. The sheet shows attributes beside derived stats, the unmet-gear list and the stat preview without scrolling at 1280x800.
  • Suits players who want to allocate points and compare gear in one glance. Costs the whole play area: the game is fully dimmed and hidden while either panel is open.
  • Tooltip lands over the other panel (it opens beside the right panel), so the sheet is partly covered during hover.
  • Effort S to M: a plain two-panel layout, the shared inventory code is reused by B and C.

B Briefcase

  • One centred case with Gear and Employee File tabs (I and C jump to a tab, arrow keys switch tabs). Strongest theme: leather, stitching, clasps and file-folder tabs.
  • Fits phone and desktop with the same structure; the Gear tab has the doll and grid side by side, the Employee File tab adds a "current kit" list. Trade-off: cannot see the sheet and the gear together, so a point spent on Grit cannot be checked against item requirements without switching tabs (the unmet-gear list is on the sheet, the "!" marks are on the gear).
  • Hides the game completely while open. Effort M (tab handling, the extra case art).

C Side drawer

  • Narrow drawers slide in from the screen edges and leave the middle of the play area visible and lit, so combat stays readable while managing gear (screen edges are dimmed only). Edge tabs and HUD buttons open them.
  • Tightest layout: cells are 38 px (A 44, B 50), the Employee File scrolls slightly at 800 px height. The tooltip opens toward the centre and can cover the game view and the belt.
  • Suits a game with constant action; the risk is small targets and a long tooltip over the game. Effort M (slide animation, tighter sizes).
Decision

Decision: inventory panel layout

Status: decided (PROXY) Date: 2026-10-13 Picked: C Side drawer Confidence: medium (high that A/C beat B on "close to the original"; medium on C over A on looks alone) Decided by: customer-proxy under the delegation in 00-brief.md. Provisional: the real customer said they want to go over screens and confirm details, so this stays open to overruling (see proxy-log.md).

Variants: A Classic split, B Briefcase, C Side drawer (see brief.md, notes.md, review-r1.md, shots/*-1280x800-compare.jpg, all looked at).

Reasons

  1. Customer words: "stay close to the original" (mechanics and feel). The genre convention is a character sheet on the left, inventory on the right, both open at once, with the game world still visible behind. C is the only variant that does all three; A has the two panels but blanks the game; B departs from the convention with tabs (hides the sheet while managing gear).
  2. The game is real-time and does not pause (see answers). Hiding the arena (A, B) while up to 50 monsters may act is a gameplay hazard. In the C shot the hero and the room stay visible and lit.
  3. Customer words: "nice graphics". All three share the C2 art direction and look good in the shots. B has the strongest theme but loses on usability (review score 3 readability, 2 composition). C ties B on total (31) and has the best composition (5). The look gap to B is closed by borrowing B's leather header, see below.
  4. Seeing the sheet change live while equipping (Damage, Health in the C shots) is the most useful feedback in the loop. B hides it.
  5. Basis is conventions plus the two quotes; nothing in the customer's words ranks "moody theme" above "see the fight". If they do, B is the alternative, not A.

Not chosen

  • A: readable and complete, but fills the screen and its tooltip covers the stats it compares (A shot: tooltip over Derived Stats).
  • B: best theme, but tabs, tooltip covers neighbouring items, game hidden.

Borrow (concrete rules)

  • From A: Employee File layout. Attributes next to derived stats, "+" targets reachable without scrolling, stat-preview note, unmet-gear list. Cells 44 px minimum. Inline rarity key with word next to the mark (mark shape + border + word + colour, NFR-A03).
  • From B: leather and stitching skin on the Desk Drawer header strip (brown strip with stitching, already echoed in the C shot); 50 px cells on phone; phone layout = one panel at a time with tabs Gear / Employee File (C's stacked phone layout hides the sheet below the fold).
  • From all: compare block with green up / red down numbers and the verdict line ("Upgrade: better in every changed stat"); "(you have 7, need 1 more)" wording; paper Employee File with the probation stamp.

Must-fix list for the implementation

  1. Tooltip never covers the bottom bar (skill slots, belt) and not the hero. Anchor beside the item toward the drawer's inner edge, cap height, flip to stay on screen.
  2. Employee File fits at 1280x800 without scrolling for attributes, derived stats and "Gear you cannot use yet" (put the unmet list above the derived stats if space is short; stats may scroll, the "+" buttons may not).
  3. Fix HUD bar badge collisions: F1-F4 and belt 1-4 badges overlap icon corners and the rarity mark of belt potions. Move badges outside or inset icons (art-direction must-fix 10).
  4. Cells at least 44 px on desktop. Check the 1024 px minimum width (NFR-B02): drawers narrow or overlap the centre, and the centre gap stays usable (at least the hero visible).
  5. Drag/drop feedback: green or red outline on the target slot with a one-line reason (e.g. "Needs Level 8"); equipped item stays visible as a dimmed ghost while dragging; held item clearly styled as "in hand"; changed derived stats flash on the sheet.
  6. Real game scene behind the drawers (the mock grey scene was a placeholder); real HUD, C2 grade, no dimming of the centre, screen edges dimmed only.
  7. Keep shared behaviour: keyboard access (tab stops, arrows in the grid), live region, focus ring, contrast >= 4.5:1, I and C toggle, Esc puts held item back.
  8. Phone: tabs as described above, targets >= 44 px.
  9. Keep all names original (R-102, R-103); no genre names introduced.

Answers to the prototyper's open questions

See the "Answers" below. Basis: genre convention where the customer is silent (stated explicitly).

  • Does the game pause while panels are open? PROXY (confidence medium): No. Real-time stays running, as in the genre; this is why C is picked. Basis: "stay close to the original"; genre convention (no pause for inventory).
  • May an item with unmet requirements be dragged onto its slot? PROXY (confidence medium): It may be picked up and hovered over the slot (the slot outline turns red with the reason, "Needs Level 8"), but the drop is rejected and the item returns to where it came from. It is never equipped. It stays in the drawer with the "!" mark. Basis: genre convention (unmet requirements block equipping, items can still be carried); R-054, brief.md interaction list ("rejection with a message").
  • Tooltip comparison for items not equippable? PROXY (confidence medium): Still shown, with the unmet line in warning style. It helps planning the next stat point. Basis: R-061, R-016.
  • Which stat point unlocks Fingerless Gloves (Agility 10)? PROXY (confidence high): Spending a point should make the "!" disappear live, and the item becomes equippable at once. Basis: R-016, QF-06-6 (requirements preview).
  • Swap on drop onto an occupied slot/overlap with one item? PROXY (confidence high): Yes, swap; old item goes to the cursor. Overlap with two items is rejected with a message. Basis: brief.md interaction, genre convention.
  • Two-handed item vs off-hand? Already decided QF-05-4: occupies the off-hand slot.
  • Real customer: "wants to go over screens and confirm details". Keep the compare shots and this decision linked in the review pack; nothing here is irreversible.

No ESCALATE items: no names, assets or legal matters were involved.
